articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses Melania Trump's diplomatic efforts, including brokering a temporary limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
First lady Melania Trump and peace envoys from both Russia and Ukraine spoke from the White House on Thursday, hailing the ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Oleshky region as a potential "spark" for peace that lasts beyond a temporary regional ceasefire.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said in a White House trilateral news conference with the two warring countries. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark."
"Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire," she added, calling Oleshky "a spark in a world of darkness capable of illuminating the best in humanity."
INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL
Trump said she became aware of a humanitarian crisis in the region in September and directed her representative, Marc Beckman, to engage with Russia and Ukraine on her behalf. She said both countries agreed to work with her as an "exclusive intermediary" to establish a ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region, deliver humanitarian aid and create a safe evacuation route for civilians.
Her remarks were followed by comments from Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev , who said Russian President Vladimir Putin appreciated President Donald Trump’s efforts to stop the fighting.
US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS
Leader of the Servant of the People political party of Ukraine, David Arakhamia, sitting side by side with Russia's presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev was a unique image at first lady Melania Trump's remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 5, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
"President Putin also appreciates President Trump's peacemaking effort and his team working on a peace plan to resolve Ukrainian crisis," Dmitriev said in a rare moment of a Russian diplomat speaking at the White House. "President Trump has asked President Putin to support a number of initiatives on exchanging of prisoners, on releasing U.S. prisoners on humanitarian efforts. And President Putin supported those ideas and those initiatives."
"And it's very important that cooperation between Russia and Ukraine and Russia in the United States matters not only for our two nations, but for the entire world," he continued. "Let us continue making great humanitarian contributions. We can together, let us build a future of peace, partnership and prosperity for the benefit of our families, our children and future generations."
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN
First lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
"Dear Melania, you saved and touched so many lives," he concluded.
David Arakhamia, the leader of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's political party, called Melania Trump's ceasefire the 'biggest de-escalation since 2022," when the war began.
UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA
"Madam first lady, I would like to thank you: You did an amazing job," he said. "I think when everything started with you and your team, we had about 5% of people who believed in success, and 95% of skeptics who said it wasn’t going to work. Now, after it happened, it’s switched completely: 95% of the people believe that we can do things like that, and 5% are still skeptical."
Peace is now a matter of when, not if, he added.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE
Signature page from Oleshky ceasefire agreement. (Provided to Fox News Digital)
Getting fearful Ukrainians out of the Russian-controlled city is an important step toward deciding how peace will be made and determining the long-term fate of the occupied territory of southern Ukraine.
"On the first day, people in the area did not believe it was happening," Arakhamia said. "They stayed in their homes, waiting to see if the clock was ticking backward. The next day, they started walking around their homes. The day after that, they came to see their broken homes and find their belongings.
"This is really emotional to watch and supervise, to understand what we are doing," he added. "I think we are creating momentum where both sides are learning the little mechanics of how to keep the peace when the peace comes.
"I would also like to sincerely thank you, from my heart, for doing this."

Dmitriev attended the event and met with U.S. officials, sources told Reuters. Dmytro Lubinets , Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, also attended the event.

articles.title_orig: Mother, daughter found dead after suspected grizzly attack
articles.title_zh: Mother, daughter found dead after suspected grizzly attack
articles.content_orig:
A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.
The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said.
Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".
Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved.
Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths.
He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.
Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC .
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable.
According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food.
But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years.
A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead.
The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.
The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017.
"With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

articles.title_orig: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.title_zh: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

articles.title_orig: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux
articles.title_zh: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux
articles.content_orig:
Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.
OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.
The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.
The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.
He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported.
Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true:
The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory.
On Alpine, accounts with no password set include:
Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas .
The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas . They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root.
Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no , and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $ -style password hash.
The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check.
OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server.
On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd:
Point releases 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 already include the fixed package. Branches 3.16 to 3.21 are past their end of support but also got fixed packages.
Cloud instances started from tiny-cloud images older than those point releases still need the update, or the setting below.
If you build OpenSSH yourself, version 10.6p2 includes the change, as its release notes describe.
If you cannot update yet, turning off password logins also stops the attack. First make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds. Then set PasswordAuthentication no , check the configuration with sshd -t , and restart sshd.
The advisory gives commands that add the setting in a drop-in file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d , which Alpine's default configuration reads from 3.19 onward. They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no , including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no .
The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine , root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys.
"If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says.
Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt() , the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field.
An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash.
For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored * , so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password.
This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks.
The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then.
The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem.
Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement , he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours.
No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.

articles.title_zh: John Deere Announces Iowa Plant Closures, Production Moves Through 2029
articles.content_orig:

This article was originally published at 1:04 p.m. CST on Wednesday, Nov. 4. It was last updated with additional information at 9:31 a.m. CST on Thursday, Nov. 5.
LINCOLN, Neb. (DTN) -- John Deere announced plans to close two Iowa manufacturing plants in the next few years and move production to other cities, in a news release from the company on Wednesday.
Deere said it will be closing its plant in Ottumwa, Iowa, after moving windrower and round-baler production to Des Moines. In addition, the company said it will end manufacturing at its Hagie plant in Clarion, Iowa, after moving STS sprayer production to Louisiana.
Windrower production plans to move to Des Moines by the end of 2027 and round balers would follow by the end of 2028, according to Deere, followed by the closure of the plant in Ottumwa.
Hagie STS sprayer production is slated to move to Thibodaux, Louisiana, beginning in 2028 with manufacturing ending in Clarion, Iowa, by the end of 2029.
John Deere told DTN the company has more than 300 workers at the Ottumwa plant and more than 200 at the Clarion facility.
When contacted by DTN for additional information, Deere said the specific employment effects will "depend on future business conditions, production volumes and staffing needs."
So, at "normal" production volumes, about 300 positions would be affected by the adjustments, Deere told DTN.
"However, John Deere is currently operating far below normal production volumes due to the downturn in the ag economy," the company said. "Employees will receive timely information as plans are finalized."
The company said it plans to provide transition support for employees at the affected facilities. That may include opportunities for workers to transfer to other plants, retraining assistance, retention offers, relocation assistance, severance benefits and career-transition support, according to Deere.
Just last week, Deere announced it anticipates hiring more than 400 people across its factories and calling back more than 275 employees to its plant in Waterloo, Iowa, according to a Oct. 30, 2026, news release from the company.
"With these callbacks, all employees previously on layoff in Waterloo, the Quad Cities, Ottumwa and Dubuque have been asked to return to work," the company said last week. "Approximately 125 employees remain on layoff in the Des Moines area."
Additionally, the company said in its latest announcement that it plans to move sugar cane harvester production from Louisiana to Catalao, Brazil, in 2029. The Louisiana plant employs between 350 and 400 people, according to information from Louisiana Economic Development. Deere told DTN that the Thibodaux move will not result in any reduced headcount at that plant, as sprayer production will be moving there.
"John Deere expects to continue serving customers without disruption throughout these changes," Deere said on Wednesday.
"The company will manage the transitions carefully with the goal of maintaining product quality, availability and service. At the same time, John Deere recognizes the impact these decisions will have on employees and communities. Throughout the transition, the company will engage with employees, union representatives where applicable, local leaders and community stakeholders, and is committed to identifying the best future use for the Ottumwa and Clarion sites."
Deere also announced plans for 2027 to move small planter production from John Deere Seeding in Moline, Illinois, to the company's facility in Paton, Iowa.
The company said it is "evaluating strategic sourcing opportunities" across its construction and forestry divisions.
"The changes reaffirm Deere's commitment to U.S. manufacturing by aligning production capacity with regional customer demand and advanced manufacturing capabilities," the company said.
"By concentrating investments in modern, high-use facilities, Deere intends to preserve and expand critical U.S. manufacturing capabilities, enhance competitiveness, support American manufacturing jobs and maintain its ability to invest through business cycles while continuing to serve customers well into the future."
In all, John Deere employs more than 12,000 people in Iowa and about 6,500 in Illinois, according to the company.

articles.title_orig: Rockstar Reveals Even More GTA 6 Screenshots as PS5 Release Draws Closer
articles.title_zh: Rockstar Reveals Even More GTA 6 Screenshots as PS5 Release Draws Closer
articles.content_orig:
You're exactly two weeks away from playing GTA 6 .
To celebrate the fact, developer Rockstar has shared another batch of screenshots that are designed to showcase Vice City at its best, and the world beyond. Take a look below at a whopping 37 new screenshots:
GTA 6 comes to PS5 on 19th November 2026, but you can get your preload started from 10th November. Learn more in our GTA 6 Release Times and Preload guide , which is staying up to date as we near launch.
A lot of the images focus on protagonists Jason and Lucia, but we do catch glimpses of other characters, the nightlife, and more that'll be part of Leonida. What's your favourite picture? Share it in the comments below.
[source rockstargames.com ]
Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.
Ok yeah these look incredible and just remember ladies and gentlemen there are people out there that think this game will flop...
It's going to be so epic, can't wait!
@Oram77 that's hilarious, it's already been pre-ordered 5-10 million copies*
Me: I'm not going to look at those for spoiler reasons. Also me: Those were some great new screenshots.
Laura Branigan said it best in Vice City, you take my self-control.
Looks amazing. Can't wait, looking forward to Digital Foundry's video also
I still maintain that this looks exactly like GTA5.
@Oram77 There’s more chance of EA winning company of the year than this game flopping.
One of the people in the screenshots literally look like Kodak Black 👀
It looks good but I'll wait on the pc release. Especially now that the normal physical edition comes without the usual goodies (map etc). Plus I got too many games to play anyway.
@LifeGirl it looks nothing like gta 5! You might need specsavers
@LifeGirl I pity your optic nerves
The texture work and level of detail on every little thing is incredible.
If the texture on the bottom of the pool in that last one is simulated rather than a loaded texture...
Ain't no way this game runs at 60FPS...
Fingers still crossed for an actual disc edition (even if it's just a licence-on-a-disc) at some point after launch.
There is every indication the game will look incredible, but even with that in mind these are still bullshots.
Am I the only one that thinks we still have not seen nearly enough gameplay yet?
Looks alright doesn’t it? I guess it’ll do for now. Plus the soundtrack is ok too I suppose.
I expect to have a moderate amount of fun playing it, repeatedly, for hours, almost endlessly. Maybe.
Not too concerned with the frame rate either, as I’ll mainly have it static just overlooking the city whilst I wan … work.
@thechetearly totally unrelated to GTA 6, but excellent taste in music! That's a great album by The Chariot, only heard it recently.
As for GTA 6, it looks fun. I'm sure it will be. But I'm not feeling a real great hype. No doubt when it floods everywhere I look it will though, and I'll buy it soon after anyway.
I just want a return of San Andreas territory system really.
Pushsquare should do an article asking readers what they plan of doing when first booting the game up. I’ll probably spend the first few days just roaming the map and seeing what random things I come across. I certainly won’t be in any rush to finish the game. I made that mistake in gta5 thinking we’d get some dlc in the coming months/years.
I've started counting days and that was the worst decision to make in this situation. Suddenly, the march towards release has slowed to a crawl and the waiting has become excruciating. I'm a victim of hype.
@LifeGirl , you clearly have not played or seen GTA 5 next to GTA 6, or you need to visit an optician urgently.
I'm not intending to buy the game, but the screenshots are very impressive. My son absolutely loved GTA 5, so I imagine that he will get it, and as we game share on the Xbox I will have the opportunity to play it should I be persuaded to do so.
I do have to say, I wonder whether it will live up to the hype, and also whether it will get fantastic 10/10 reviews whilst at the same time numerous issues with the game are pointed out? I wonder whether professional reviewers will feel compelled to give the game 10/10s, or whether it will deserve them, and whether those same issues in another game would see it marked down? In other words, is the game too big to be critiqued properly?
I'm sure the game will be good, but will it be as good as we will be led to believe? I hope it is for the sake of all those that are really looking forward to it, but as someone on the outside of the hype, the excitement is kind of bewildering. To me, it's a bit like everyone raving about the latest Artic Monkeys album, when I just don't like their music and I cannot understand how anyone does... 😉
Laura Branigan, @GirlVersusGame ? Are you an old soul or just well versed on good music? I was there front of the queue to buy her first album when it released in 1982. I absolutely loved her...
All at a staggering beautiful 30fps. My time is on Zelda OOT.
@Oram77 game has already done $750 million in sales and it's not out yet. It can't literally bomb. But it can be a massive let down enough to shake the entire gaming foundation. I don't think it will be. But I still hold reservation for performance issues plaguing this game from when CD showed 48 minutes of Cyberpunk "gameplay" and we all know how that turned out at launch.
@AI-Generation I'll be playing both
As I'm still waiting for a 60fps mode for RDR2 before buying it, I'll probably buy and play GTA6 on a second hand PS6 Pro.
@Fiendish-Beaver Music is a kind of obsession and Vice City, along with many other games in the series helped to introduce me to so many good bands and musicians. Music is a big part of why I want to experience Six. I tend to prefer older music, movies and people. You definitely experienced the better timeline.
@Oram77 That’s fantastic, I’m not sure about GTA6 shall wait and see, as you know I have the 30fps hump 🤣
@Boxmonkey I bet that if you took a random landscape screenshot from both games and put them side by side you would not be able to tell the difference.
Can’t wait. It’s all ready. Ps5 pro, LG G5 and my Soundsystem. My only concern are the 30 fps, especially on an OLED. We will see how this turns out. Even it’s absolutely unrealistic: still having a glimpse of hope for any kind of 40 fps mode.
Grand theft auto i6 is going to be a instant and win game of the year. Word up son
Only 2 more weeks! Also getting my new ( and slightly bigger 😁 ) Oled next tuesday, so im ready for GTA6.
Yea hyped to play this now, lm away in switzerland sunday before it releases till the friday so that should make the time go faster 🤣. As soon as im back on friday it will be on all weekend and not moving only for food drink and toilet 🤣. Im glad we havent had too many trailers for it, can go in relativley blind to it.
@LifeGirl get real! There is a huge difference between gta5 and rdr2. I understand trying to be contrarian but this is taking it a little too far.
Hold on there, you need to login to post a comment...

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) stocks extended declines on Thursday, each dropping roughly 9%. Shares of the Elon Musk-led companies were pounded after Democrats won control of the House and Senate this week, raising concerns over regulatory hurdles for data center buildouts in the US and merger aspirations between the two companies.
The Democratic win in Texas, where both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered, is at the center of the concern. The state flipped blue at the gubernatorial level and saw the Senate seat won by James Talarico, with whom Musk got into fierce spats on social media leading up to the elections.
"We will believe a SpaceX/Tesla merger happens but now faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap to get this deal done in 2027 given this new political blue roadmap in DC/Texas," Yorkville's partner and managing director Dan Ives wrote on Thursday.
Elon Musk said on SpaceX's third quarter earnings call last month that he thinks merging the company with Tesla ( TSLA ) would be a good idea and revealed that both companies are exploring a potential deal.
Earlier this year, Musk also announced the launch of a Terafab, a massive semiconductor manufacturing complex in Texas that would supply SpaceX and Tesla.
Worries over a slowdown in data center build-outs also dampened shares of Texas-based SpaceX, which has increasingly leaned into AI compute as a revenue source.
Ives said while Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed $1 trillion in 2027, the growth rate into 2028 "will clearly moderate significantly as the data center buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map, especially in the state of Texas."
On Wednesday, Goldman Sachs analysts also calculated, "Democratic wins at the state and local level are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion.

articles.title_orig: Wonder Restaurant App Files Confidentially to Go Public
articles.title_zh: Wonder Restaurant App Files Confidentially to Go Public
articles.content_orig:
Food startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said Thursday.
Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place," available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app.
Originally envisioned as a new take on food delivery through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens, Wonder has grown to roughly 170 brick-and-mortar locations throughout the U.S. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants" across a variety of cuisines, some with branding from celebrity chefs.
Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own restaurant business based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders.
Wonder has spent at least $1 billion on acquisitions, such as delivery service Grubhub, meal kit brand Blue Apron and delivery and logistics provider Relay, along with some buzzy restaurant concepts. Wonder has been able to afford such expensive dealmaking thanks to more than $3 billion in venture funding.
Wonder's Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion.
With the proceeds from an IPO, Wonder will be able to make more acquisitions and work toward its goal of making food more accessible, Lore told CNBC in September.
But as a public company, Wonder will also likely face investor scrutiny. Weak consumer sentiment has weighed on restaurant stocks recently, plus market volatility has resulted in a shaky IPO market for companies across a range of industries.
Lore previously founded Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart, respectively.

articles.title_orig: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Stock Today Has These 2 Positives. The Stock Is Still Falling.

articles.content_orig:

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. SPCX shares have fallen 17.8% in the past month even as third-quarter growth, profitability and earnings estimates improved sharply. The pullback has made the stock cheaper, but it has not resolved the debate around capital intensity and execution. Shares are still up 6% over the past three months. That contrast suggests investors are reassessing how much future growth is already reflected in the valuation as spending accelerates.
Third-quarter revenues surged 161.4% year over year to $14.58 billion, while operating income reached $2.79 billion against a $273 million loss a year earlier. Net income improved to $4.40 billion from a $1.05 billion loss. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current fiscal year has also moved sharply higher, with the four-week earnings estimate change at 106.2%. Still, a better operating picture must be weighed against an investment program that is expanding faster than internally generated cash.
Connectivity revenues rose 69.5% year over year to $5.25 billion, helped by Starlink consumer subscribers reaching 13.6 million. Enterprise and government revenues climbed 91% to $2.13 billion, broadening the segment beyond consumer subscriptions. Super Intelligence revenues jumped 829.9% to $7.56 billion. New cloud services agreements, the Cursor acquisition and growing Grok adoption drove the increase, while segment operating income turned positive at $431 million after a $1.72 billion loss a year earlier.
Third-quarter capital expenditures reached $19.59 billion, including $16.44 billion for Super Intelligence infrastructure. For the first nine months of 2026, capital spending totaled $48.07 billion versus $13.10 billion of operating cash flow. Management expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of $35 billion to $40 billion as additional compute capacity comes online. SpaceX had about $89.86 billion in cash and marketable securities at September-end, but the scale of planned investment keeps capital efficiency central to the return outlook.
Starship Flight 14 reached orbit and deployed 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites, but major milestones remain. SpaceX still must demonstrate recovery of both stages, orbital refueling, rapid reusability and a much higher launch cadence to support its broader expansion plans. Rocket Lab Corporation RKLB provides useful launch-sector context through its Electron launch business and developing Neutron vehicle. AST SpaceMobile, Inc. ASTS is building a space-based cellular broadband network for standard smartphones, making it relevant as SpaceX expands Starlink Mobile.
The pullback improves the entry price, but the stock still reflects a difficult balance between fast growth and unusually heavy spending. Sustained returns depend on Starship execution, continued Starlink expansion and profitable utilization of rapidly growing compute capacity. SPCX currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). Its Momentum Score of A is its strongest Style Score, while the Value Score of F, Growth Score of C and VGM Score of D point to a less favorable mix across valuation and broader growth characteristics. That combination supports a measured stance rather than treating the one-month decline alone as a buy signal. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here .

articles.title_orig: California-based restaurant chain operator files for bankruptcy as it blames state’s brutal wage laws
articles.title_zh: California-based restaurant chain operator files for bankruptcy as it blames state’s brutal wage laws
articles.content_orig:
A major California-based Outback Steakhouse franchise operator has gone bust, blaming the Golden State’s soaring labor costs, sky-high food prices and dwindling customers for pushing its restaurant empire to the brink.
San Diego-based Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, also known as Out West Restaurant Group, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Monday in Delaware, seeking relief from a staggering $449 million debt burden, according to the Los Angeles Times .
The struggling company operates 61 Outback Steakhouse restaurants across California, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico, with the majority of its locations concentrated in the Golden State.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
And company executives say California’s punishing minimum wage requirements have only made an already brutal financial situation worse.
California’s statewide minimum wage jumped to $16.90 an hour in January, while fast-food chains have been required to pay workers at least $20 an hour since 2024.
Although Outback Steakhouse is exempt from the higher fast-food wage mandate, its operators still face mounting payroll expenses under the state’s broader wage laws.
More than half of Cerca Trova’s employees work in California, according to bankruptcy filings.
“By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged,” CEO David Goronkin said in court documents cited by the Times. “Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise.”
The company’s financial woes have been brewing for years.
Its debt has ballooned from approximately $269 million in late 2020 to $449 million this year, as inflation, rising operating expenses and shrinking customer traffic hammered its bottom line.
Even the chain’s signature steaks have become increasingly expensive to serve, with beef prices climbing as much as 5% annually since 2022, according to court filings.
The franchise operator was once Outback Steakhouse’s largest franchisee, boasting 99 restaurants in 2018 before shrinking to its current 61 locations.
Among California locations that have recently shut down: 7575 Beach Blvd. in Buena Park, 25261 N. The Old Road in Valencia and 26652 Portola Parkway in Foothill Ranch.
Now, the company is looking to unload its remaining restaurants in a court-supervised sale.
Outback parent company Bloomin’ Brands has emerged as the leading bidder, offering $26.3 million to acquire the struggling operator’s assets unless another buyer comes forward with a better deal, per Newsweek .
The Florida-based restaurant giant has also agreed to provide up to $5.5 million in financing to keep the franchisee afloat during bankruptcy proceedings.
Bloomin’ Brands insisted the financial meltdown was limited to the franchise operator and would not disrupt its broader business.
A Bloomin’ Brand spokesperson told the Post the bankruptcy is “an isolated situation involving the franchisee and does not affect Bloomin’ Brands’ corporate operations, financing, or liquidity.”
The filing marks another blow to California’s battered restaurant industry.
A major Carl’s Jr. franchise operator, Friendly Franchisees Corporation, recently sought Chapter 11 protection through subsidiary Sun Gir, citing California’s $20 fast-food minimum wage as a significant contributor to its financial troubles.
The wage hike’s economic consequences remain fiercely debated, with critics arguing it has squeezed restaurant operators while supporters maintain its impact has been limited.
Meanwhile, casual-dining chains nationwide have been struggling to lure inflation-weary Americans back through their doors.
Red Lobster filed for bankruptcy in 2024, while Oprah-backed True Food Kitchen recently sought Chapter 11 protection and shuttered three Southern California locations.

Outback has also experienced declining foot traffic, with parent company Bloomin’ Brands reporting a 2.8% year-over-year drop in customer visits during the second quarter.
For now, the steaks will keep sizzling at Cerca Trova’s restaurants, even as the company fights to survive its financial crisis.

articles.title_orig: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control
articles.title_zh: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control
articles.content_orig:
Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase 's banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year.
Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel's thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation's biggest bank has not been announced.
The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel's ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield.
Democratic staffers aim to focus in particular on decisions about Epstein made by Mary Callahan Erdoes, the CEO of JPMorgan's asset and wealth management division, the source said.
JPMorgan declined to comment. The bank has previously said it regrets any association with Epstein but that it did not assist him in committing crimes.
In a 2023 deposition , Erdoes said she was aware as early as 2006 that Epstein was accused of paying cash to have underage girls brought to his home. Epstein had been a client of the bank since 1998.
Epstein became a registered sex offender after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to a state criminal charge of procuring an underage girl for prostitution.
JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon in his own, later deposition in 2023, said Erdoes had authority to cut off Epstein as a client. She did not take that step until 2013.
Epstein, a former friend of President Donald Trump , ex-President Bill Clinton and many other high-profile people, died in a jailhouse suicide in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on federal child sex trafficking charges.
A lawyer for the U.S. Virgin Islands told a federal judge in New York in 2023 that JPMorgan "was a full-service bank for Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking," and that it waited until after he killed himself to notify the Treasury Department of $1 billion in suspicious transactions related to trafficking by Epstein.
"This was a CYA [cover your a--] reporting after 16 years of all of the monies flowing in his JPMorgan accounts after he was dead," the lawyer, Mimi Liu, said.
JPMorgan has blamed former investment banking chief Jes Staley for concealing or failing to report criminal activity related to Epstein, with whom he had a close relationship.
Staley, who left JPMorgan in 2013 and later became CEO of Barclays before stepping down in 2021, has denied knowledge of Epstein's crimes.
House Oversight Chair James Comer, R-Ky., after a closed-door interview with Staley in July, said that the former executive had encouraged JPMorgan to keep Epstein as a client.
In mid-2023, JPMorgan agreed to a $290 million settlement with victims of Epstein without admitting wrongdoing. That same year, JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to settle a separate lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands alleging that the bank facilitated and benefited from the sex trafficking of young women by Epstein.
In August, Wyden released a report accusing top officials at multiple banks of "looking the other way" as Epstein moved hundreds of millions of dollars to finance a yearslong sex trafficking operation.
"The report exposes how top bankers shielded Epstein from federal scrutiny by delaying the reporting of Epstein's suspicious financial activity to the U.S. government, likely in violation of federal anti-money-laundering laws," Wyden's office said in a statement that month.
"It includes new details about the extent of suspicious activity reported by Deutsche Bank after Epstein's death, new details from bank reports filed about suspicious transfers to Epstein through accounts at Bank of America, and names top officials at JPMorgan Chase and other banks who were responsible for reporting Epstein's shady activities to the government but instead protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black and other billionaires."
Black, former CEO of Apollo Global Management, was revealed to have paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice in the years after his 2008 conviction.
In September, Black sued the House oversight panel, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued him for his testimony and for documents related to its Epstein probe.
On Wednesday, Black sued Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chair of the Oversight Committee in the next Congress, alleging Garcia defamed him in statements regarding Epstein. The lawsuit focuses on Garcia's claims in a TV interview that Black "is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes" and "was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before his death, among others.
The Department of Justice's mountain of files related to Epstein became a major focus in late 2025 and early 2026, after Congress passed a bill ordering the DOJ to make those records public.
Trump's name is referenced thousands of times in the files that have been released.
The president has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he fell out in the early 2000s.

articles.title_zh: Wendy's turned down Nelson Peltz's $1.4 billion offer. It's betting instead on thicker bacon and whole-leaf lettuce.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wendy's ( WEN ) new CEO Bob Wright just revealed his plan to save the ailing fast food chain, and it looks a lot like the one Burger King ( QSR ) ran to rack up huge sales in 2026.
The plan hinges on a return to better food quality if fast food diners are going to pay inflationary prices.
"We are also rebuilding our food offerings and have begun testing improvements to quality and craveability of our core items, including thicker, crispier bacon, a richer and creamier Frosty, whole leaf lettuce on sandwiches, and improved salads," Wright said on his earnings call Thursday morning.
Wendy's conviction in its turnaround attempt, called Dave's Way, has led the company to reject a $1.4 billion buyout offer from billionaire investor Nelson Peltz's Trian Partners.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Wendy's board chair Art Winkleblack wrote in a statement . "Our confidence rests firmly in Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds."
The company will have a lot of work to do to turn around the struggling fast food business.
In the third quarter, Wendy's reported US same-store sales declined 5.7%, marking the company's seventh straight quarter of comparable sales declines, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis.
Wendy's reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.13, beating Wall Street's estimates of $0.09. Third quarter revenue of $547 million declined 0.5% year over year but came in ahead of the Street's estimate of $531 million, per S&P Global Market Intelligence.
The restaurant chain has also been dealing with franchisees shuttering locations amid severe margin pressures. In September, Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection following an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters.
Wendy's said Thursday it plans to acquire up to 163 Wendy's restaurants from Meritage.
"WEN appears to have aligned the system around Dave's Way, altered its approach to breakfast and has plans for greater portfolio changes, all of which should help the longer-term story," Citi analyst Jon Tower wrote in a note. "However, this will be overshadowed by potential M&A headlines and short of WEN indicating M&A is off the table, we see a floor on share performance today."

articles.title_orig: The leader of a German conservative party is found dead at a Berlin hotel
articles.title_zh: The leader of a German conservative party is found dead at a Berlin hotel
articles.content_orig:
By SABRINA PENTY, FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 04:33 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 05:57 EDT, 5 November 2026
A German conservative politician has been found dead at a Berlin hotel less than 24 hours before he was set to deliver a speech.
Hubert Aiwanger, 55, the leader of the conservative Free Voters party , was found lifeless in his room at the Neuer Fritz hotel on Wednesday evening after people close to him had failed to make contact with him, German newspaper Bild reports.
Police cars and several state government cars were pictured outside the hotel yesterday evening.
Mr Aiwanger, Bavaria's deputy governor and the southern state's economy minister, had planned to deliver a speech on Wednesday afternoon at the opening of a Berlin office of his party, but pulled out of the event for health reasons, according to reports.
An investigation into the cause of death was opened.
Spokesperson for Berlin's public prosecutor's office Michael Petzold told Bild that 'nothing can be ruled out at this point'.
The newspaper reported that Mr Aiwanger's body had no external injuries.
Mr Aiwanger had been the party's leader in Bavaria since 2006 and its national leader since 2010.
Conservative politician Hubert Aiwanger has been found dead at a Berlin hotel
A police vehicle is seen outside the Neuer Fritz hotel in Berlin, Germany, on November 4, 2026, where Aiwanger was found dead
An investigation into the cause of death was opened
The combative politician with a strong regional accent and a populist touch made his party a serious rival to Bavaria's long-dominant Christian Social Union (CSU), which is part of the centre-right bloc that currently leads Germany.
On his watch, it entered the state legislature in Munich in 2008.
Ten years later, when the CSU lost its majority in the state legislature, it entered Bavaria's government as the junior coalition partner.
Shortly before Bavaria's 2023 election , Mr Aiwanger faced a furore that started with allegations – denied by the politician – that he was responsible for an antisemitic flyer when he was a high school student 35 years earlier.
His party supports Ukraine in its war with Russia, and believes Kyiv should have its full, pre-war territory restored.
The Free Voters emerged unscathed from the election, having gained support and remained part of the state government.
Mr Aiwanger's party has made only limited inroads outside Bavaria, and he wasn't able to lead it into the national parliament.
Bavarian governor Markus Söder wrote on X that 'the sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy'.
A statement on the regional government's website said it 'mourns' the loss of Mr Aiwanger.
Mr Söder has ordered flags to be flown at half-mast on all state government buildings in Bavaria.
Mr Aiwanger is survived by his partner, Free Voters politician Tanja Schweiger, and their two children.
This is a developing story; more to follow.

articles.title_orig: BoE hikes rate for first time in 3 years; retreating oil prices may allow for more options ahead
articles.title_zh: BoE hikes rate for first time in 3 years; retreating oil prices may allow for more options ahead
articles.content_orig:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years as it warned that inflation is surging towards 5pc.
Policymakers voted to raise rates to 4pc from 3.75pc on Thursday in the first increase since August 2023.
The Bank blamed the ongoing conflict in the Middle East for triggering another sharp jump in energy prices, with John Healey’s maiden Budget doing little to ease a two-year decline in household incomes.
Threadneedle Street now believes inflation will peak around 5pc by the middle of 2027, even if the economy slows sharply.
However, policymakers said price rises would hit 6pc next summer if the Iran war drags on.
The Bank also laid bare the impact of the conflict on family finances, with Donald Trump’s war pushing up mortgage costs for the average household by £1,500.
The Ofgem energy price cap is now expected to rise by more than £400 to £2,150 in January, with the Chancellor’s £100 Budget handout doing little to mitigate the increase.
Andrew Bailey said growing price pressures from the prolonged war in Iran meant Thursday’s increase was unlikely to be the last.
Other members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the prospect of another rate rise before Christmas.
One member, Catherine Mann, called for an immediate 0.5 percentage point jump to 4.25pc.
Thanks for following our coverage of the Bank of England’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.
Andrew Bailey said there was a “strong” case for more rate rises as the Iran war ramps up inflation pressures on the economy.
You can keep up to date with the latest here .
Analysts at Goldman Sachs were surprised by the signals from the Bank of England that more interest rates were likely.
Andrew Bailey said he could “see the argument of a further increase in rates”, with fellow policymakers Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill and Megan Greene also indicating further increases were on the cards.
The views of other rate setters also surprised Goldman.
James Moberly, an economist at the Wall Street bank, said: “We had not expected Catherine Mann to support a larger hike, and had anticipated that Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra would prefer to hold.”
The FTSE 100 in London remains up 0.7pc despite the Bank of England signalling more interest rate rises could be on the way.
However, US tech stocks continued their falls this week in the wake of the midterm elections.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged 1.2pc to 25,427.44 at the open on Wall Street, while the benchmark S&P 500 fell 0.4pc to 7,654.89.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5pc to 53,595.12 as investors switched out of tech stocks into more traditional sectors, over fears the Democrats would limit expansion of AI companies.
Traders expect too many interest rate rises from the Bank of England over the next year, an investment manager has warned.
April LaRusse, co-head of client portfolio management at BNY Investments, said money markets were anticipating too many further rate rises.
Traders are betting that the Bank will raise rates to 4.75pc by the end of next summer.
She said: “While we believe today’s increase was important in reinforcing the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility, markets may now be somewhat too aggressive in the scale of further tightening they are pricing.
“Growth continues to benefit from strong business investment, particularly around AI-related infrastructure, but beyond this area we expect the economy to soften through 2027.
“Against that backdrop, the hurdle for further rate increases is likely to rise after the initial few hikes.”
Telegraph readers said inflation feels much more severe than the Bank of England’s forecasts of around 5pc in the early months of next year.
Here are some views from the comments section below and you can join the debate here .
Households face a “clear risk” that the Bank of England will raise interest rates in December after putting up borrowing costs for the first time in three years on Thursday.
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said the “balance of risks has shifted” in favour of higher inflation, after policymakers forecast prices could rise at an annual pace of around 5pc early next year.
He said the latest rate rise was an “insurance policy” against the risk of inflation rising further and said he did not expect several increases in the future.
But he warned: “The bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February.
“There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).”
Andrew Bailey, coming towards the end of his press conference, said he hopes there will be more information on whether the Iran war will end by the Bank of England’s next meeting in December.
Answering a question from Telegraph economics editor Szu Ping Chan , he said: “We will judge this at each meeting.
“We will inevitably have more information by December because we will get more data releases and so on.
“I hope we will also have more information on where this conflict is going to. That would be the most important thing.”
Andrew Bailey said he “could see the case” for a further quarter point increase in interest rates to 4.25pc if the Middle East war is not resolved.
The Governor also said he would not sign up to suggestions that households faced just two rate rises as a result of the war.
“I’m not going to sign up to the two-and-done point,” he said.
Any further increase in interest rates would come down to “risk judgement”.
He said: “Things have happened in the last 48 hours but the whole situation is so volatile that we really don’t want to put much weight on two days, which frankly haven’t yet been backed by any firm evidence that there is a peace process which is going to lead to something concrete.”
Traders are betting it is a coin toss whether the Bank of England will raise interest rates for a second time before Christmas.
Money markets suggest there is a 53pc chance policymakers will vote for the Bank Rate to be lifted for a second meeting in a row to 4.25pc in December.
Traders had given a second rate rise this year a 30pc chance before the Bank announced it was raising rates from 3.75pc to 4pc.
However, they increased bets on higher rates after Andrew Bailey, the Governor, said there was a “strong” case for a second rate rise if the Iran war was not brought to an end.
John Healey has been urged to cut benefits and lower taxes after inflation rose to 4pc.
Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Rising interest rates are another headwind for hardworking families to deal with.
“They mean higher mortgage costs, and with the independent OBR confirming that living standards will fall next year, it’s time Labour cut taxes, welfare spending and costly regulations to make life cheaper for families.”
“The tax burden is expected to hit a record high in the wake of Mr Healey’s first Budget last week.”
Andrew Bailey called for an end to the Iran war to end the inflation pressure facing households this winter.
The Governor of the Bank of England said he was unable to tell people how high interest rates would go but said the best way to resolve price pressures in the economy was for the Middle East conflict to come to an end.
He said: “Inflation is bad for everybody... it is most difficult for those on low incomes and those struggling to find work.
“We are very conscious of the need to deal with this.
“In conditions that are as uncertain as the ones we face, I cannot give any assurances to people about where are interest rates going to go to.
“All I would come back to... and this was the same message as the Prime Minister gave yesterday, actually, which I firmly agree with, the focus must now be on dealing with this conflict, ending this conflict.

articles.title_orig: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
ROME — The EU is giving the impression of being “all over the place” when it comes to Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told European Council President António Costa.
In a letter seen by POLITICO, Meloni said that discussing how the EU can speak with one voice on Ukraine should be added to the agenda of an informal leaders’ meeting in Dublin next week, adding that the issue “can no longer be postponed.”
Meloni pointed out the various formats that have been used to discuss Ukraine, including meetings in Miami and Oslo, and upcoming talks scheduled by the Coalition of the Willing and the European Political Community, plus the phone call that Finland’s Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre made to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. She said the multiple forums were “undermining our credibility in handling one of the most complicated issues our nations are facing.”
While the EU has repeatedly insisted it gets a “seat at the table” at Ukraine peace talks, to  safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Kyiv’s ability to resist a lopsided deal, the bloc has yet to agree on a single leader or institution to spearhead negotiations.
“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue,” the Italian prime minister wrote. “And I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake.”
“Proceeding in a disorganized manner, with initiatives that chase one another and overlap, will not help us — neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to stop this senseless aggression,” she added.
“I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format,” she said.
EU leaders meet in Dublin for an informal European Council on Nov. 13. A meeting of the European Political Community, which involves all EU states plus Ukraine and other allies, takes place the day before.
As the format for talks increasingly coalesces around the E3 — the U.K., France and Germany — alongside the EU, NATO and Ukraine, Italy has found itself sidelined.
Rome was excluded from meetings in Miami in October and Brussels this week, although it did take part in talks in Oslo at the invitation of the Norwegian government. An Italian national security adviser attended a working dinner there, but Italy’s participation came in place of France, rather than as an additional seat at the table.
Over the past year, Italy has emerged as the EU’s most vocal and persistent advocate for appointing a special envoy for Russia-Ukraine peace talks. Meloni first publicly floated the proposal in January, arguing that the bloc needed to “speak with one voice” and engage directly with Moscow.
While other countries, including France, Austria, Czechia and Luxembourg, have also expressed support for the idea, Rome has led the push, with Italian officials repeatedly raising it on the sidelines of EU summits and in discussions among EU ambassadors preparing leaders’ meetings.
Ahead of the latest EU summit in October, Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani seized an opportunity during an exchange with reporters at a European People’s Party pre-summit gathering to renew the call for a special envoy.
Asked whether Costa himself should take on the role, Tajani praised him but insisted that the priority was for Europe to have “a spokesperson who can negotiate” and articulate a “univocal position,” warning that otherwise EU foreign policy would appear weak.
Gerardo Fortuna and Elena Giordano contributed reporting. This article has been updated.
